{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>

{{Short description|Form of Japanese pagoda}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2021}} {{Italic title|reason=}} [[File:Ishiyamadera29n4272.jpg|thumb|300px|Tahōtō at [[Ishiyama-dera]], dating to 1194 and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]]; distinctive features are the square base; [[stupa]] mound; [[mokoshi]] or lower 'skirt' roof; upper pyramidal roof; and ''[[sōrin]]'' or [[:en:Finial|Finial]]]] [[File:Houtou - Ankokuron-ji.jpg|thumb|150px|A ''hōtō'']] [[File:Negoroji-daitou-flooplan.svg|thumb|150 px|Floorplan of the [[Tahōtō#Daitō|daitō]] at [[Negoro-ji]]; many features are shared with the ''tahōtō''; the daitō is larger, with five [[Ken (architecture)|bays]] on each side rather than three]] [[File:Ryukoji03.jpg|thumb|right|150px|{{nihongo|[[Stupa]]|仏舎利塔|''busshari-tō''}} at [[Ryūkō-ji (Fujisawa)|Ryūkō-ji]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]; without a protective roof, the [[plaster]] weathers rapidly]] [[File:Sagamiji04s3200.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Tokyō|Four-stepped brackets]] at [[Sagami-ji]], [[Hyōgo Prefecture]]]] [[File:Iwawakiji tahoto sorin.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Bronze ''sōrin'' or finial at Iwawaki-dera, [[:en:Ōsaka Prefecture|Ōsaka Prefecture]]; comprising an inverted bowl, [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals, nine rings, flame, and [[Cintamani|jewel]]]]
A {{nihongo|'''''tahōtō'''''|多宝塔|lit. many-jewelled pagoda}} is a form of [[Japanese pagoda]] found primarily at [[Vajrayana|Esoteric]] [[Shingon]] and [[Tendai]] school [[Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]]. It is unique among [[pagoda]]s because it has an even number of stories (two). (The second story has a [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]] and seems habitable, but is nonetheless inaccessible and offers no usable space.)<ref name="nk">{{cite book |title=Nihon Kenchiku-shi |editor=Fujita Masaya, Koga Shūsaku |publisher=Shōwa-dō |date=10 April 1990 |edition=30 September 2008 |isbn=4-8122-9805-9 |language=ja |ref=CITEREFFujitaKoga2008 }}</ref> Its name alludes to [[Prabhutaratna|Tahō Nyorai]], who appears seated in a many-jewelled pagoda in the eleventh chapter of the [[Lotus Sutra]].<ref name="Houtou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/h/houtou.htm |title=Houtou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="Nicoloff"/> With square lower and cylindrical upper parts, a ''[[mokoshi]]'' 'skirt roof', a pyramidal roof, and a [[:en:Finial|Finial]], the ''tahōtō'' or the larger ''daitō'' was one of the [[Shichidō garan|seven halls]] of a [[Shingon]] temple.<ref name="Daitou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/d/daitou.htm |title=Daitou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> After the [[Heian period]], the construction of pagodas in general declined, and new ''tahōtō'' became rare. Six examples, of which that at [[Ishiyama-dera]] (1194) is the earliest, have been designated [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasures]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp |title=Database of National Cultural Properties (多宝塔) |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> There are no examples in [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|China]], whether [[Chinese architecture|architectural]] or [[Chinese painting|pictorial]], of anything that resembles the ''tahōtō'', although there is a [[Song dynasty]] textual reference to a '''tahōtō'' with an encircling chamber'.<ref name="Soper">{{Cite book |title=The Evolution of Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Soper, Alexander Coburn |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1942 |pages=194–7}}</ref>
==Hōtō== The {{nihongo|''hōtō''|宝塔}} or treasure pagoda is the ancestor of the ''tahōtō'' and dates to the introduction to Japan of Shingon and Tendai Buddhism in the ninth century.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Soper"/> No wooden ''hōtō'' has survived, although modern copies do exist. They are usually made from stone, bronze, or iron, and specimens are always miniatures comprising a foundation stone, barrel-shaped body, pyramid roof, and a finial.<ref name="Houtou"/><ref name="Tahoutou">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tahoutou.htm |title=Tahoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref>
==Daitō==
While the ''tahōtō'' is 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|ken]] (bays), a larger 5x5 ken version exists, known as {{nihongo|''daitō''|大塔}} or 'large pagoda'.<ref name="Daitou"/> This is the only type of ''tahōtō'' to retain the original structure with a row of pillars or a wall separating the corridor (''[[Hisashi (architecture)|hisashi]]'') from the core of the structure, abolished in smaller pagodas.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref name="Hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=74|language=ja}}</ref> ''Daitō'' used to be common but, of all those ever built, only a few are still extant. One is at [[Wakayama prefecture]]'s [[Negoro-ji]], another at [[Kongōbu-ji]], again in Wakayama, another at Kirihata-dera, [[Tokushima prefecture]], another at [[Narita-san]] in Chiba. (See the respective list entries.) [[Kūkai]] himself, founder of the Shingon school, built the celebrated ''daitō'' for [[Kongōbu-ji]] on [[Kōyasan]]; almost fifty metres high, chronicles relate that 'the mightiness of its single storey outdoes that of multi-storeyed pagodas'.<ref name="Nicoloff"/><ref name="Soper"/><ref name="Mikkyo"/> The specimen found at Negoro-ji (see photo above) is 30.85 meters tall and a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]].
==Structure==
===Single-storey=== [[Japanese pagoda|Japanese pagodas]] have an odd number of stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/t/tasoutou.htm |title=Tasoutou |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> While the ''tahōto'' may appear to be twin-storied, complete with [[:en:Balustrade|Balustrade]], the upper part is inaccessible with no usable space.<ref name="nk" /> The lower roof, known as a ''[[mokoshi]]'', provides shelter and the appearance of an additional storey.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/mokoshi.htm |title=Mokoshi |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Floor plan=== Raised over the {{nihongo|''kamebara'' or 'tortoise mound'|亀腹}}, the ground floor has a square plan, 3x3 [[Ken (architecture)|''ken'']] across, with a circular core.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kamebara.htm |title=Kamebara |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> Inside, a room is marked out by the {{nihongo|''shitenbashira'' or 'four pillars of heaven'|四天柱}}, a reference to the [[Four Heavenly Kings]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Tahoutou"/> The [[Gohonzon|main objects of worship]] are often enshrined within.<ref name="Tahoutou"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/shitenbashira.htm |title=Shitenbashira |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref>
===Upper part=== Above is a second 'tortoise mound', in a residual reference to the [[stupa]].<ref name="Soper"/> Since exposed [[plaster]] weathers rapidly, a natural solution was to provide it with a roof, the ''mokoshi''.<ref name="Soper"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Early Buddhist Architecture in Japan |author=Suzuki, Kakichi |publisher=[[Kodansha]] |year=1980 |ISBN=0-87011-386-0 |pages=18f}}</ref> Above again is a short, cylindrical section and a pyramidal roof, supported on [[Tokyō|four-stepped brackets]].<ref name="nk"/><ref name="Parent">{{cite book |title=The Roof in Japanese Buddhist Architecture |author=Parent, Mary |publisher=Weatherhill |year=1983 |ISBN=0-8348-0186-8 |pages=128, 292f}}</ref>
===Finial=== {{main|Sōrin}} Like all Japanese pagodas, the ''tahōtō'' is topped by a vertical shaft known as the {{nihongo|''sōrin''|相輪}}.<ref name="Sourin">{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/s/sourin.htm |title=Sourin |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=23 May 2011}}</ref> This comprises the base or 'dew basin'; an inverted bowl with attached [[Padma (attribute)|lotus]] petals; nine rings; 'water flame'; and [[Cintamani|jewel]].<ref name="Sourin"/> The finial's division in sections has a symbolic meaning and its structure as a whole itself represents a pagoda.<ref name="hamashima group">{{cite book|last=Hamashima|first=Masashi|title=Jisha Kenchiku no Kanshō Kiso Chishiki|year=1999|publisher=Shibundō|location=Tokyo|pages=224|language=ja}}</ref>
==Miniature versions== A number of smaller versions of the ''tahōtō'' are known, of stone, bronze, iron, or wood, and similar to the ''hōtō''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721084842/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/937 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724132830/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5183 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 July 2012 |title=Database of National Cultural Properties |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=23 May 2011 }}</ref>
==Meaning== A number of [[mandala]] show the Iron Stupa in southern [[History of Buddhism in India|India]], where the patriarch [[Nāgārjuna]] received the [[Mahavairocana Tantra|Esoteric scriptures]], as a single-storey pagoda with a cylindrical body, a pyramidal roof, and a spire.<ref name="Soper"/> The forms used in the ''tahōtō'', namely the square, circle, triangle, semi-circle, and circle, may represent the [[:en:Five elements (Japanese philosophy)|Five Elements]] or the [[:en:Five Precepts|Five Virtues]].<ref name="Nicoloff">{{cite book |title=Sacred Koyasan: A pilgrimage to the Mountain Temple of Saint Kōbō Daishi and the Great Sun Buddha |author=Nicoloff, Philip L. |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |year=2008 |ISBN=978-0-7914-7259-0 |pages=124–131, 301–3}}</ref><ref name="Soper"/> The egg-shaped [[stupa]] mound or [[aṇḍa]] may represent [[Mount Sumeru]], with the finial as the axis of the world; or, by a folk interpretation, the square base may represents a folded robe, the dome an overturned begging bowl, and the spire a [[Kongō-zue|walking staff]].<ref name="Nicoloff"/> The ''tahōtō'' served not as a reliquary tower but often as an icon hall.<ref name="Tahoutou"/>
